chapters.title: Chapter 1: How Business Income Gets Taxed in India

lessons.title: Proprietorship, Partnership, LLP or Company: How Your Structure Changes Your Tax Bill

body.text: Two businesses can earn the same profit, sell the same product and employ the same people, and still hand over very different amounts of tax. The difference is the legal box the business sits in, and that box is chosen on day one, usually by someone who has not yet read a tax law.

children.text: India taxes a business according to what it legally is. A proprietorship is not a separate taxpayer at all, so its profit is simply the owner's income. A partnership firm and an LLP are separate taxpayers at a flat rate. A company is a separate taxpayer too, but with a catch: getting the money out of the company triggers a second tax. This lesson shows what each choice costs.

body.caption: How each structure is taxed on business profit

cells: No, profit is the owner's own income
Personal slab rates, up to 30% plus surcharge and cess
Free. Drawings are not a taxable event
Partner's share of profit is not taxed again. Remuneration and interest are, within limits
22% base under section 200 [old 115BAA], or 25% / 30% in the old regime, plus surcharge and cess
Dividend is taxed again in the shareholder's hands. Salary is deductible for the company

body.text: A One Person Company is a company for tax purposes, not a fancier proprietorship. It pays corporate rates and faces the same second layer of tax on dividends. Founders who register an OPC expecting proprietorship-style simplicity are often surprised.

children.text: The Rate Is Only Half the Story: One Layer or Two

A company's 25.17% effective rate looks cheaper than an LLP's 31.2%, and for profit that stays inside the business it genuinely is. But a company's profit belongs to the company, not to you. Moving it into your own bank account as dividend means paying personal tax on it as well, at your own slab rate, with tax deducted at source by the company under section 393 [old 194].

body.title: ₹100 of company profit, fully paid out as dividend to an owner in the 30% slab

body.label: Combined tax when a company pays out all its profit
body.context: 25.17% at the company, then 31.2% (30% plus 4% cess) on what is left. An LLP paying the same profit to its partner stops at 31.2%. Surcharge is ignored here for clarity.

children.text: Take a Surat textile trading business run by one owner. It earns ₹40,00,000 of profit before paying the owner anything, and the owner wants the whole amount in her personal account this year. She has no other income and is taxed under the default personal regime in section 202 [old 115BAC].

body.caption: Same ₹40 lakh profit, three legal structures

cells: LLP, entire profit retained as her share
Private limited, entire profit paid as dividend
Private limited, ₹24 lakh salary plus dividend

body.title: Show me the math behind all three routes

children.text: The LLP pays 30% plus 4% cess on ₹40,00,000, which is ₹12,48,000. Her share of the remaining profit reaches her without a second tax, so she keeps ₹27,52,000.

content.caption: Rupee amounts. The 22% base rate under section 200, grossed up by 10% surcharge and 4% cess

children.text: That leaves ₹29,93,280 as dividend. Under the section 202 slabs, the first ₹4 lakh is nil, and the next five slabs of ₹4 lakh each are taxed at 5%, 10%, 15%, 20% and 25%, adding up to ₹3,00,000 of tax on the first ₹24 lakh. The remaining ₹5,93,280 is taxed at 30%, or ₹1,77,984. Tax before cess is ₹4,77,984, and 4% cess takes it to ₹4,97,103.

Salary is a business expense, so paying herself ₹24,00,000 leaves the company with ₹16,00,000 of taxable profit and tax of ₹4,02,688. The remaining ₹11,97,312 comes to her as dividend. Her personal income is ₹35,97,312, reduced by the ₹75,000 standard deduction available on salary, so ₹35,22,312 is taxed: ₹3,00,000 on the first ₹24 lakh, then ₹11,22,312 at 30%, which is ₹3,36,694. With 4% cess, her tax is ₹6,62,162.
Employer contributions to provident fund, professional tax and the cost of running each structure are ignored here, as is surcharge, which does not apply at these income levels.

body.text: Route 3 is not a free lunch. Salary must be genuine and reasonable for the work actually done, backed by a board resolution and an employment agreement, with TDS deducted every month. An LLP faces its own ceiling: section 35(e) [old 40(b)] allows the higher of ₹3,00,000 or 90% of the first ₹6,00,000 of book profit as partner remuneration, then 60% of the balance, and interest on partner capital only up to 12% a year. Anything above those limits is disallowed, so the entity pays tax on it anyway.

body.title: Try It: The LLP Route
body.prompt: An LLP earns ₹60,00,000 of taxable profit and pays no remuneration to partners. At 30% plus 4% cess, what is its tax for the year? Answer in ₹ lakh.
body.explanation: ₹60,00,000 × 30% = ₹18,00,000, and 4% cess adds ₹72,000, giving ₹18,72,000 or ₹18.72 lakh. That is an effective 31.2%. Surcharge of 12% would apply only if income crossed ₹1 crore.

children.text: What the Law Asks of Each Structure
Tax rate is one cost. Compliance is another, and it is the one small businesses feel every month.

Yes, under the Companies Act as well
Turnover above ₹1 crore, or ₹10 crore if cash receipts and payments are within 5%. Professionals at ₹50 lakh
Above prescribed turnover or contribution limits

body.text: From tax year 2026-27, the tax audit report moves to a single Form No. 26, replacing Forms 3CA, 3CB and 3CD. Section 63 also brings a quieter change: a business declaring profits below the presumptive rates in section 58 can be pushed into audit even if it never opted for the presumptive scheme.

body.title: Quick Check: Which Profit Gets Taxed Twice?
body.question: Four owners each pull ₹10 lakh of business profit into their personal account. Whose money is taxed at the entity level and then taxed again in their own hands?
options: The proprietor taking drawings from her proprietorship
The partner taking his share of an LLP's profit
The shareholder taking a dividend from her private limited company
The partner taking his share of a partnership firm's profit
body.explanation: Only the company route has two layers. A proprietor's drawings are not a separate taxable event, because the profit was already her personal income. A partner's share of firm or LLP profit is not taxed again once the entity has paid tax on it. A dividend, however, is taxed in the shareholder's hands at her slab rate on top of the company's own tax.

columns.label: LLP suits you when
points: You want most of the profit in your own hands each year
The business is service-led, with few external investors expected
You value lighter compliance and no statutory audit at smaller sizes
Professional practices and family-run consultancies are typical examples

columns.label: A private limited company suits you when
points: Profit will be reinvested rather than withdrawn, so 25.17% beats 31.2%
You plan to raise money from angels, VCs or a bank that wants a company on the other side
You want to grant ESOPs, which need share capital
You expect to sell the business one day, since share transfers are cleaner than reconstituting a firm

body.title: Scenario: The Kochi Software Studio
body.scenario: Two engineers run a software studio as an LLP. It earns about ₹80 lakh of profit a year, all of which they take out for personal use. A venture fund now wants to invest ₹5 crore, and the founders want to grant stock to the first ten employees.
body.prompt: Should they stay an LLP or convert to a private limited company, and what changes on the tax side?
body.modelAnswer: On pure tax, the LLP is doing well right now. At ₹80 lakh of profit taken out every year, they pay about 31.2% in total, whereas a company distributing everything as dividend would cross that once personal slab tax on the dividend is added. But the funding and ESOP plans decide this. Venture funds invest in equity shares with rights that an LLP cannot issue, and ESOPs need share capital, so a conversion to a private limited company is effectively required. After converting, the tax picture changes: the company pays about 25.17% under section 200 [old 115BAA] on profit it retains, which is now the plan anyway since growth capital is being raised to reinvest rather than distribute. The founders should also move to drawing reasonable salaries, which the company can deduct, rather than relying on dividends. They should plan the conversion carefully, because the tax law attaches conditions to converting a firm or LLP into a company, and take professional advice before filing.

body.text: A common founder mistake is treating a company's bank account as a personal wallet. A loan or advance from a closely held company to a substantial shareholder can be treated as a deemed dividend and taxed in that shareholder's hands, even though nobody declared a dividend. Once the business is a company, the money inside it is genuinely not yours until it is paid out properly.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: Money Out of a Firm
body.textWithBlank: When a firm or LLP pays its partner remuneration or interest above ₹20,000 in a year, it must deduct TDS at ___ percent under section 393(3) [old 194T].
body.explanation: Section 393(3) of the Income-tax Act, 2025, which carries forward section 194T of the 1961 Act, requires 10% TDS on salary, remuneration, commission, bonus or interest paid to a partner once the total for the year crosses ₹20,000 for that partner. A partner's share of profit is outside this, because it is not taxed in the partner's hands.

body.title: Choosing a Structure: Questions to Answer Before You Register
steps: How much of the profit will you actually withdraw each year, and how much will stay in the business?
Will you need outside equity investors, ESOPs or a formal board within the next three years?
What is your expected turnover, and does it cross the tax audit thresholds in section 63 [old 44AB]?
Are you eligible for the presumptive scheme in section 58 [old 44AD, 44ADA, 44AE], and does it simplify your life enough to matter?
Can you sustain company-level compliance: statutory audit every year, Registrar filings and board meetings?
Does a customer, lender or tender process require you to be a company in the first place?

cards.definition: The concessional corporate regime: a 22% base rate for domestic companies that give up most deductions, or about 25.17% after surcharge and cess.
The default personal tax regime and its slabs, running from a ₹4 lakh exemption up to 30% above ₹24 lakh.
Caps how much remuneration and interest a firm or LLP can deduct for payments to its own partners.
Requires a firm or LLP to deduct 10% TDS on remuneration, commission, bonus or interest paid to a partner above ₹20,000 in a year.
The presumptive taxation scheme, which taxes a percentage of turnover instead of actual profit. Not available to LLPs or companies.
The tax audit requirement, now reported in Form No. 26, triggered mainly by turnover thresholds.
A loan or advance from a closely held company to a substantial shareholder that is taxed as if it were a dividend.

points: A proprietorship is not a separate taxpayer, so its profit is taxed at the owner's slab rate and drawings are tax-free
Firms and LLPs pay a flat 30% plus surcharge and cess, and the partner's share of profit is not taxed a second time
A company pays about 25.17% under section 200 [old 115BAA], but dividends are taxed again in the shareholder's hands, taking the combined burden to roughly 48.5%
Salary to a founder-director is deductible for the company, which is why a salary plus dividend mix usually beats an all-dividend payout
Firms and LLPs face their own ceiling on partner remuneration and interest under section 35(e) [old 40(b)], and 10% TDS under section 393(3) [old 194T]
If profit is reinvested, or outside investors and ESOPs are on the horizon, a company wins despite the second layer of tax

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax or legal advice. Rates, thresholds and section references reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 as understood at the time of writing, with the corresponding 1961 Act section shown in brackets. Provisions change with each Union Budget. Verify current rules or consult a qualified chartered accountant or company secretary before choosing or changing a business structure.
